purpose: Acarbose is used to help control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It works best when used along with a healthy diet and exercise. Sometimes it is used together with other diabetes medications like metformin or insulin.
how_it_works: When you eat carbohydrates like bread, pasta, or rice, your body normally breaks them down quickly into sugar, which causes your blood sugar to spike. Acarbose slows down the enzymes in your intestines that break down those carbohydrates. This means sugar enters your bloodstream more slowly and gradually, keeping your blood sugar from rising too fast after meals.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are stomach-related — things like gas, bloating, diarrhea, and stomach pain or cramps. These happen because undigested carbohydrates sit longer in your gut. These side effects are usually worse at first and often get better over time as your body adjusts.
warnings: If your blood sugar drops too low (hypoglycemia) while taking acarbose — especially if you are also on insulin or certain other diabetes pills — you must treat it with plain glucose (like glucose tablets or gel), NOT regular fruit juice or table sugar, because acarbose will slow the absorption of regular sugar. Tell your doctor if you have any liver or kidney problems, or any bowel or digestive diseases, as acarbose may not be safe for you. Your doctor may check your liver enzymes periodically while you are on this medication.
typical_dosing: Acarbose is usually started at a low dose — 25 mg taken three times a day with the very first bite of each main meal. Your doctor will slowly increase your dose over a few weeks, typically up to 50 mg or 100 mg three times daily, depending on how your body responds and your blood sugar levels. Always take it with food — it will not work properly if taken on an empty stomach.
